segments.text: Namaste, Jai Hind, Vande Matram.
Welcome to yet another edition of Take 3 with the usual suspects here, Nalin Mehta, Rahul Shiv Shankar and Anand Darsaman.
Let's try and dive into two different subjects, both quite varied but both which will perhaps pinch our pockets or impact us in our daily lives.
So let's begin with the latest first.

The latest is Donald Trump getting perhaps, after he signs off on it, unbridled powers to impose up to 100% tariffs on nations like Bharat, China, and those including Hungary and Azerbaijan, who are buying a lot of oil and gas from
Russia and especially when it comes to oil, the top five importers of oil, they can be taxed up to or tariffed up to 100 percent.
But will Trump take this bite?
Can he afford to take this route going forward with both Bharat and China?
Before these wise old men, if I may say, are able to or weigh in with their wisdom,
I would just like to say I'm happy that Bharat is being bracketed with China.
So that is somewhere a coming of age and turn of the page that Bharat is being bracketed with China.
That means we are already at the table.
We don't need to try any more viewers.
That's my simple reading from a non-strategic point of view or from a layman's point of view.
But Nallin Mehta, let's start with you.
This tariff and these bills, this man has by hearted them.
He rattored them.
Usually, you are the one who's rattored everything, but in this case, he knows the bill, you know, like the back of his hand.
So, we'll get to him in a bit.
From your point of view, are you in favour of the American Congress actually passing something like this, especially when there is a view from both sides that the Bharat-US ties have been
stitched together over the last two decades and they could all be upended if someone like Trump who is like a bull in a china shop is given such powers.
So India's statement on this today is a very strong statement.
It specifically talks about the interest of 1.4 billion people.
It makes the point about energy security.
It says that all necessary measures will be taken to safeguard India's security.
I think this is the strongest statement we have seen so far from the MEA.
It changes the narrative so far as it was.
I think India has kind of done a lot of negotiation behind the scene on this.
We have refrained from taking on the Americans publicly on this.
This is a strong statement today.
Two or three things.
Number one, it is very clear talking to senior people in the government that there's unlikely to be a rethink on Russian oil supplies.
In fact, India, Russia's oil supplies have actually increased year on year.
If you see the latest month's data, which is available compared to a year ago, it's gone up from about 38% to about 41%.
That's one.
Two, India is also simultaneously looking to diversify.
Look, but there are very few alternatives around, right?
And you also have a crisis in the Strait of Hormuz.
So I don't see India backing off from this.
A, B, this certainly has an impact on the optics of the negotiation.
Now, what has happened in the US?
This bill has been passed, it's gone to Trump.
They're going to use it as leverage in the negotiation again.
India has made a public position, made it very clear.
I think the challenge for India is going to be that if you look at the trajectory of this vis-a-vis China, you mentioned China at the beginning of your statement.
If you see over the last 12 months, when the first time tariffs were put on India for Russian oil, 25% was put on India.
China at that time was importing more than India was.
Zero was put on China.
That was in August 2025.
6th of August.
On the 27th of August, 2025, 50% was put on India.
That time, again nothing was put on China.
On the 7th of February, 2026, few months ago, additional 25% was removed, reciprocal tariff was cut to 18%, no action on China.
The reason is that China has always had far more leverage than India has had.
in terms of strategic metals and all of the rare earth and all of that.
And also buying their corn.
The farmers, their own crop was upended because about 10 to 15 billion dollars of China said, I'm not buying from you.
At the moment, India is somewhere around 60 days of oil in its strategic reserves.
You take crude and process both.
India is working on building that capacity.
But I don't see India backing off from this.
In fact, the month of August, the number is 51% of India's energy is being supplied by Russia because of the oil crisis that we are facing.
But yes, Mr. Shivshankar.
So there are two or three different things that I want to bring together.
First of all, let's look at clause 3 of the Ministry of External Affairs.
Two gentlemen are competing for notes.
The MEA has said this issue has been discussed at high levels in recent months with various US interlocutors.
Now comes the important part.
its potential implications for not just the bilateral relationship, but also the international energy market have been very clearly articulated by the Indian side.
Bilateral relationship.
You do this, there are going to be implications.
We will move in another direction.
Secondly, the international energy market.
Now why has this been used?
This is a very important and loaded phrase and I've just done some research.
See together India and China purchased 3.3 million barrels per day from Russia.
Russia is a big oil supplier globally.
Russian oil I think is in the top three.
So Russia is out there selling a lot of oil.
If India and China stop buying Russia, what happens?
Russia will tighten production.
It will lead to scarcity of oil internationally.
When is this scarcity going to hit?
When the Saudis are having a difficulty now sending oil to Europe.
So you just don't have two buyers.
China and India looking for other alternatives to avoid sanctions if we were to do that.
But you also have the EU saying, oh, our Saudi oil is not coming or is not coming in gushes.
We've got to look around.
What does that mean?
You have more demand than supply.
The first thing that happens is oil prices spike.
Yeah.
Okay.
And that has an effect on freight, fertilizer and food costs, fueling global and US inflation.
So US inflation, which is already up there, beyond the Fed level of 2%, recommended level, it's already about 3 point something.
So that's a problem.
It's a political problem and a headache for Trump.
Now, when is all of this going to hit?
When the Fed is hiking interest rates?
So there's less money that's going to go into the market to expand businesses.
There's a 10-year treasury yield at about 5%.
It just came down a little bit under 5% today, but it's been hovering around that number, which means, once again, the cost of borrowing for U.S.
businesses has gone up, right?
So U.S.
businesses are going to sort of say, if you want to expand, this is not the right time.
And most importantly, you have a situation where global growth is also going to be hit.
So what happens?
Punishing India and China will rebound first on the US because there will be stagflation in America.
Globally, there will be stagflation.
So punishing India and all of that, you want to roll up your sleeves and you want to say, OK, Modi and OK, Xi.
So what I'm trying to say is that you ask me this question, will Trump dare he has to think it through?
Now, I'm not saying, and it'll be too simplistic to say, oh, 3.3 million barrels will just disappear off the market.
You see, Trump could approach it in a different way.
He could go for increasing premiums on insurance.
He can hit in other places.
He can hit private companies and entities.
He doesn't have to hit India.
It's a complete, I don't want to use the word, esho.
Yeah, it's a complete esho, but will that be allowed is one point.
Yeah.
Nalin, you want to say something?
I want to make a point that it's not just about India and China.
They are the significant buyers of Russian oil.
Turkey is the other one.
A lot of stuff goes to EU as well.
Egypt is also a very big buyer of Russian oil.
Turkey is a NATO ally.
We are not hearing any noises about that.
So the targeting of India is also a political move.
If you look at the data, China actually buys more than India, right?
But we are not hearing voices against China as much as you are hearing against India in Washington.
You're hearing much more against China.
You're not hearing about Turkey.
You're not hearing about EU.
You're not hearing about Egypt.
So there is a lot of politics behind this.
So the answer in this is not a technocratic answer.
The answer in this is that this is a political game, right?
And in that sense, India is showing that it has more options.
India, which is why I think the BRIC Summit was very important.
Modi holding hands with Putin and Xi Jinping was an important signalling for that reason as well.
True, I agree, but there are multiple layers to this.

One is that there is a huge Indian diaspora in the US, which contributes significantly to the American economy, and somewhere there will be this backlash of trickle-down racism, which will spill over.
That's one point that Bharat will have to contend with, because the Prime Minister has very clearly said that even the Indian diaspora outside matters to him.
But obviously, the interest of the 1.4 billion people here is important.

The other thing is, somewhere when they talk about bilateral ties, do you think now Bharat is a little more confident, especially after this BRIC Summit, that there are alternative markets for trade, there are alternative markets for fuel, and there is a non-west option, which Bharat will seriously start exploring now going forward, if Trump
you know, exercises the tariff option.
Now he talked about the fact that and you also said that China was not taxed or tariffed.

Now China was not tariffed because China hit back at such a way that it was it really was a sucker punch for Trump because his own core voter base said my bumper crop has been upended because of your policy.
So sort that out.
So he had to sort it.

The other part is will the world now call out American hypocrisy because nearly five point five billion worth of uranium and rare earth minerals and etcetera is being purchased from Russia by America itself.
He's also given a free pass to the entire European group of nations who are also NATO allies because they want to buy energy, gas from Russia.
And they are the ones who are fighting this war against Russia and for Ukraine.
So this whole hypocrisy, will it be called out?
And does this perhaps strengthen the RIC combined?
Do we see more Chinese investment?
Do you see opening doors with China and say, okay, let's park our adversarial attitude there?
A huge amount of opening that has happened with China in the last few months in the lead up to the BRIC Summit.
You only have to look at the size of the delegation and the companies that came.
Huawei was here.
Huawei has been shut off from the American market.
And the fact that Huawei was part of the delegation, it was signaling as well.
I don't see the rest of the world calling out too many things because the rest of the world is already very unhappy with the Americans, but they can't do much.
Look at the Europeans.
How unhappy they've been with Trump in the last few months.
But I think
It really is realpolitik.
It really is to the strong the world in that sense.
I mean, I think the older rules are gone.
As far as India is concerned, we may not have options to retaliate or effective options to retaliate, but we certainly have the resilience to look at other options.
And I think there is clear determination at the top of the government on not backing off on Russian oil.
I don't see India reducing the Russian oil immediately as a result of threats, certainly.
No, I have a slightly different view.
I just feel that Trump will not go ahead with this 100% business.
India is already showing that, look, we have cut back on Russian oil.
In any case, look, let's be honest, Russian oil is not coming to us with the concessions.
It's now in a dollar and a few cents.
It's not giving us those five or eight dollars margins that we were getting earlier.
So fundamentally you have to look at it from that point of view.
Is it worth antagonizing the US?
But since we have our issues, and you know, just today, and in the next two, three days, there are military exercises going on with the United States.
RIC is a great place to be.
Yes, it's great for leverage, but outcomes, there's no convergence.
Consensus, yes, you can have, yes, you know, the Americans, and you can have this nice fancy statement which can, you know, poke the Americans in their side, but there's no convergence of interests.
And our relationship with China is a completely one-sided trade relationship.
So we need a market for our goods.
Rahul has got a point about whether Trump will pull the trigger or not.
But it certainly gives him a further lever in negotiations.
I don't want any nation to try and think that they can get away with bullying us.
It's not going to happen.
Sorry.
And yes, what is going to happen?
There will be short-term pain, some trades, etc.
But okay, the European Union is also not very happy with Trump.
In respect to what Ursula von der Leyen says, look at the comments he made when they want to meet Canada and associate members.
So they have their own tussle going on.
And there are nations who are looking to India to say, especially in the global south, who are looking to say, can this guy stand up to the bully?
Can he stand up to America and get there?
Because then it gives them confidence to also stand up and say, all right, we also will not agree.
So and then it has to force our markets to say, we will look at other options.
We look beyond America till the time because who's to know it all started under Biden.
It's continued with Trump in a far more abrasive manner.
The next person may continue to act.
Actually, Biden made exceptions for us when it came to trading.
Realizing that India was doing actually a human service.
It all started with Biden's advice to buy oil from Russia.

And I think the Foreign Minister has already made it clear that not only did they make exceptions, there was a conversation between the Americans and us and they specifically asked us to stabilize the energy markets.
Because they said we want the Gulf oil for Europe, so you buy from Russia for some time.
That's what they said.
Back then, at least, America was in a slightly better position.
Now, whether you give Trump credit for bringing back the American economy by not going in for those long lockdowns and shutdowns during COVID, etc., etc., America was doing pretty decently.
Biden inherited quite a vibrant American economy.
Now things have changed because of this war.
It's been the biggest global oil shock since the 1970s, so let's not be dismissive about that.
That's why I was saying, the odds are stacking up against Trump.
He pulls the trigger now, he hits American consumers, American businesses.
I remember heading into an election, he's heading into a November election.
Where they're looking a bit dicey.
The American hegemony also, the sway will be hit because a lot of them people will decamp and say, I've had enough of this bully.
And at least somewhere where the sentiment is enough.
I'm not going to take this kind of stuff from him.
Having said that, it is a piquant situation for India to be in.
Let's not minimize the dilemma and the piquancy of the situation.
This is not a quagmire that you want to be dragged into.
It's a sticky situation and also politically, if the optics are that you're negotiating with a gun to your head, the political cost of that is high.
We also have to see how President Xi games this, how China games this.
Obviously, they have far greater leverage over the US.
But how they game this system and what happens when he visits or whether or not he visits next for the summit, that's the big question with the bilateral with President Trump if he visits the US.
We'll see what happens there.
We've got limited time, so I just quickly want you gents to weigh in on the UPI fee, the MDR.
What's a quick take?
take on this.
Why don't you start first?
I am just very clearly saying, I believe that if you... Age before beauty.
So says the beast.
Okay, we are digressing.
Let's just look at this fact that at the end of the day, is this going to widen the indirect tax net bracket?
as long as more people come under the tax and I'm okay.
Otherwise, it's all on the middle class.
That's the sentiment I get.
GST bhi tum bharo, income tax bhi tum bharo.
Ab UPI free tha, usk par bhi tumar au par transaction tax hai, wo bhi tum bharo.
Yes, UPI was not free pre-COVID.
It was not free.
They made it free so that they can expand it free.
Yes.
But all banks are making money.
All payment apps have got various ways to make money.
The government is making so much of money.
That's what they have money.
So why is it that they cannot bear this cost?

Why are they saying that I can spread UPI from a base of 500 million and take it to a billion only if you allow a levy of, and if it is going to be only on 4% of the entire value chain of UPI, then why do it in the first place?
Can I wait?
Sir, the cost of operating UPI, the entire architecture is 20,000 crores as we speak.
We are being told over the next two years, 500 million more customers are going to be added.
That cost is only going up.
The government is subsidizing to 2,000, 18,000 crores.
The companies are absorbing these great companies.
That 2,000 crores even, if tomorrow you were to go down this route,
You'd be killing the entire UPI by making it almost impossible for these companies to continue to do this business, number one.
Number two, you said it was free till 2019 or what have you.
It's never been free.
If you are actually subsidizing, if the government is subsidizing, whose money are they using?
They're using my money, your money, the middle class money.
So you're okay with your tax money instead of going to build hospitals and schools and nicer streets and public infrastructure goes to subsidize, hang on, private companies who are making profits?
No, why should they pay?
Let those private companies pay for it.
Why shouldn't they?
The point is, the base is only 4% of the entire value.
96% their government is saying is below 2000 rupees.
There is no MDR there.
So 4%, this 4% you think is going to earn them 20,000 crores.
I think the issue... No, there are other avenues which will come to it.
Yes, go ahead.
The issue, Anand, politically for the government now on this is that, look, they are saying, okay, 95 percent, 96 percent of transactions are exempt.

I think the issue politically, the challenge is the optics of this, A. B, while on the one side it allows smaller players, fintech players to come in and all that, and for large investments, can you really make it global all that, the way Rahul is saying.
On the flip side, the real challenge, I think the confusion lies in the number of multiple categories of exceptions that have been put in the thing.
So people are confused.
If you had one thing, either this or that.
I'll give you an example.
There's a one lakh limit for smaller merchants, right?
Now, with that, so that they're not, so four percent
of transfers for merchants are less than 2000 rupees by volume.
But when you look at it by value, 67% are like that, right?
So if you are going to a Sabziwala for example, how would actually, and you also now have to pay GST for above that.
So it becomes, people will find it complicated to deal with it and that is where the poor
If you go to a petrol bank, you don't have to pay extra money because it's 5 rupees, the dealer charges fixed at 5 rupees.
So at a petrol bank percent to merchant, there is no MBR.
You don't have to do any calculation, you have to calculate for every transaction.
There is no MBR now, even at the petrol bank, there is no, it's going to remain 5 rupees only.
It's going to be a standard and the merchants are already paying.
It's not from that.
I'm just saying, what are you achieving out of this?
Your volume or value is not as much for you to cover this 20,000 crore expense.
It's not going to cover that money.
What money?
There are, you know, the broking fees.
That's going to amount to a substantial amount.
Now, whether they'll be passed on, I'm not sure.
Okay, because there is this whole business of various people being told that they can't pass on.
No, they could.
See, broken fees, convenience fees cannot be passed.
I am just asking you today.
Look at the number.
He said 67% value.
So, sorry, it's just 70%.
Let's say the total number is 92,000 crores is transacted via UPI on a daily basis.
Okay, that's the number.
92,505, that's the diagonal value of UPI transactions every day.
Not the volume, the value.
So, in 2025-26, more than 24,000 crore UPI transactions worth 314 lakh crores.
No, no, I am saying per day.
I am talking about 92,000 crores per day.
So, in that 70% you are saying is below the 2,000 rupee threshold.
So, 70% you remove.
So, what you are getting, you still have about 30-40,000 crores rupees per day.
25 to 30,000 crore rupees per day is still being transacted.
In that 30,000 crore rupees, 0.4 of that 30,000 crore is how much?
No, so it's about 120 crore.
29 lakh crore was the value of UPI transactions in August.
70% were person-to-person payments.
Correct.
30% was person-to-merchant.
Merchant.
Now in this also, there is a category.
So you're saying that number is further lower.
It will be 10,000 to 15,000 crore rupees.
Yes.
In 15,000 crore rupees, it's not even 60 crore rupees per day because 40 paisa per 100 rupees.
That's what it is.
But that's 18,000 crores at the end of the year.
No, how?
do the math.
So that comes to exactly the number that we need.
So basically the government will make roughly around 2000 crores on this.
Now you can make the argument that does it is that in a 50,000 in a much larger budget which is India runs a very large budget.
Is that a... Do you really need to do that?
Or can you just continue to subsidize it?
I think that's an argument.
There are two sides to both that, to that argument.
But fundamentally, a choice has now been made.
I think it is politically a difficult choice that has been made.
And there is a lot of blowback on it.
And we are still feeling the anger on the streets of that blowback.
Yeah, but the point is, the other thing is that the government has not been able to very ably give the example that when we do a credit card transaction, we are paying up to 4%.
Debit card transaction is 1.5%.
Here it is 0.4%.
But the same middle class that you are talking about, that is whinging supposedly about this, is cool about paying 4%.
See, that's exactly what I'm trying to say.
You've not been able to explain this to people.
You've not been able to explain this to people because that is a cost I'm already paying.
See, that's a communication problem.
Now look, the point is that whether it's the opposition that is now demanding a rollback, it has been proven that in the parliamentary committees, they supported all of this.
They realized the problem.
They realized that the government cannot be bailing out.

Yeah, I know, we've got to wrap, we've run out of time, so they understand they cannot do it, but have they all communicated it wrong and have they done it at a time when everything that the government does, there is a sense that it is against the middle class and it is against the Aam Aadmi.
So, you know, at that kind of a time, have you pushed forward for something like this?
Once you're used to getting something free for a while, no matter what the argument, you will always win if you've taken it away.
If you've got to pay for it.
Whether the argument is right or wrong.
Alright, thank God we're not paying for the chai at least so far in office.
Thank you very much.
Bye.
